parsed.title: Autonomous Driving: End-to-End Learning, Imitation Learning, and Simulation
outline: Comparison of CNN and RNN Architectures
Simulation Tools for Training and Validation
Gaps and Challenges in Current Research
parsed.markdown:
Autonomous driving research employs various approaches including end-to-end learning and mid-level representation methods. ChauffeurNet, an RNN model, uses mid-level input representations to output driving trajectories, enabling training on both real and simulated data and facilitating closed-loop simulation testing prior to real vehicle deployment [1]. The CARLA simulator is an open-source platform designed for autonomous driving research, supporting development, training, and validation of urban driving systems with flexible sensor suite and environmental condition specifications [2]. CARLA also provides free urban environment content such as layouts, vehicles, buildings, and pedestrians, and offers measurements of agent state and traffic rule compliance [2].

End-to-end learning approaches include convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that learn the entire processing pipeline to steer an automobile directly from single front-facing center camera images, generating steering commands [3]. CARLA has been used to study end-to-end imitation learning alongside other autonomous driving approaches, supporting training and validation of perception and control models [2].

The CNN-based end-to-end method and the RNN-based mid-level representation method differ fundamentally in their input and output representations. The CNN generates steering commands directly from raw images, whereas ChauffeurNet outputs driving trajectories based on mid-level inputs [1,3]. ChauffeurNet incorporates components such as FeatureNet and AgentRNN, with recurrent feedback mechanisms to improve predictions [1].

Simulation platforms like CARLA align well with mid-level representation approaches by enabling controlled scenario evaluation and closed-loop testing before real-world deployment [1,2]. This combination supports safer and more flexible development workflows.

Despite these advances, there is a lack of direct empirical comparison between end-to-end CNN and mid-level RNN approaches under consistent conditions or datasets [1,3]. Additionally, pure imitation learning has been found insufficient even with large datasets and mid-level representations, due to error accumulation and distribution shift during closed-loop operation [1]. However, it remains unclear whether end-to-end approaches overcome these limitations, indicating a gap in understanding the comparative effectiveness of different imitation learning strategies [1,3].
